The Story, Promise, and Future
of the Churches of Christ

The class title, as every week. Then the chapter.
Our Wild Democracy · Chapter 3

Declaration and Address,
part two

Title up. → “Last week we set the Declaration and Address in its history. Tonight, Campbell’s answer.”

Christendom’s search for unity

One church.
Recap. One click per division: creeds and confessions, councils, emperors and magistrates, bishops and popes. Every one was offered as an instrument of unity; virtually every one failed, and often created the very division it meant to overcome. Last click: the egg breaks.

Why did every instrument fail?

Card. Fifteen hundred years of creeds, councils and swords, and a document that despairs of the old way. The next slide names the reason underneath.
Anton von Werner, Luther at the Diet of Worms, 1877 · public domain
Worms, 1521

Conscience cannot
be compelled.

Asked to recant. (“Here I stand, I can do no other” is the famous form; the earliest printed accounts add it, the transcript does not. Say “as the story goes.”)
→ This is why no instrument on the egg could work: a creed can name who agrees, and a sword can make people say it, but neither can make anyone believe.
Here I stand

“…my conscience is captive to the Word of God. I cannot and will not recant anything, since it is neither safe nor right to go against conscience.”

Martin Luther at Worms, 18 April 1521
• The line everyone remembers. Say it slowly. (“Here I stand, I can do no other” is the famous form; the earliest printed accounts add it, the transcript does not.)
• → Then what conscience is, and the whole sentence it ends.
Not incidental

“Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.”

Acts 5:29
• Not an incidental fact: a deep fact about Christianity itself. The church taught its people that God is obeyed before any human authority, and so every attempt at consensus by committee or council meets someone who says, “I cannot.”

Every instrument of unity meets someone
who says: I cannot.

Pope, emperor, council, creed: “here is where you must come.” And someone always stands where Luther stood. That is why they fail, over and over.
Luther did not invent this

Even a mistaken
conscience binds.

Thomas Aquinas, c. 1270 · paraphrased
Aquinas, two and a half centuries before Worms, Summa Theologiae I-II q.19 a.5 (“whether an erring conscience binds”): “every will at variance with reason, whether right or erring, is always evil.” Even believing in Christ, willed against one’s reason, is evil.
→ Rome condemned Luther; it never stopped teaching this.
(Avoid the Aquinas line about dying excommunicated, Sentences IV d.38: its meaning is disputed.)
“A human being must always obey the certain judgment of his conscience.”Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1992
“He must not be forced to act contrary to his conscience.”Vatican II, 1965
Two clicks. The same teaching, in Rome’s own words today.
• Catechism §1790 continues: “If he were deliberately to act against it, he would condemn himself.”
• Vatican II, Dignitatis Humanae §3 (Catechism §1782): “No merely human power can either command or prohibit acts of this kind.”
• The honest gap: Gregory XVI, Mirari Vos (1832), called liberty of conscience for everyone “that absurd and erroneous proposition.” Rome reached Campbell’s conclusion in 1965.
→ Back to the egg: you can compel conformity; you cannot compel communion.
Worms · 1521

Rome rejects Luther.

Four slides, no clicks, one beat each. Same rhythm every time; let the room hear the pattern before you name it. Rome: excommunication (January 1521), then the Edict of Worms (May 1521) makes him an outlaw.
Marburg · 1529

Luther rejects Zwingli.

The man rejected at Worms, eight years later: “You have a different spirit.” No common table over the bodily presence.
Zurich · 1527

Zwingli rejects the Anabaptists.

His own students, Grebel and Manz, over infant baptism. Zurich’s council, with Zwingli’s support, made rebaptism a capital crime (March 1526); Felix Manz was drowned in the Limmat, 5 January 1527, the first Protestant executed by Protestants. The picture is from the Martyrs Mirror, the Anabaptists’ own book of martyrs: an Anabaptist held under at the riverbank, as Manz was in the Limmat. (Zurich’s own chronicle shows Manz’s drowning too: Heinrich Thomann’s 1605 copy of Bullinger.) Two years later, at Marburg, Zwingli would ask Luther for the hand he had refused Manz.
Each one was rejected for his conscience, and each one rejected the next man for his.
Washington, Pennsylvania · 1809

How dare you put asunder?

Then Campbell, turning Proposition 9 on all of them: “Whom God hath thus joined together no man should dare to put asunder.” Not one of the four was rejected for denying Christ. Each was rejected by a brother. Pause before moving on.

Luther claimed conscience for himself.
Campbell claimed it for his brother.

Say it once and stop. Not a new principle: the same principle, extended to the brother. Luther is not the villain here: the man of Worms and the man of Marburg were equally sincere. That is the point: conscience claimed for yourself is only half a sentence, and Campbell finishes it. This is the chapter in one line.

Freedom of conscience is how Christ
has put his body together.

Campbell’s move: the inability to compel conscience is not a roadblock on the way to unity. It is a constituent element of the body of Christ, an organizing principle of the church. To thwart it is to undo what Christ has done.
Preamble

“…as no man can be judged for his brother, so no man can judge for his brother; every man must be allowed to judge for himself, as every man must bear his own judgment—must give account of himself to God.”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• The Preamble’s second sentence: the half Luther could not say at Marburg. Not a right claimed but an impossibility stated: you cannot believe for someone else. Zurich and 1806 on the egg were the magistrate trying. The first sentence, just before it: “it is high time for us not only to think, but also to act, for ourselves… to this alone we feel ourselves Divinely bound to be conformed, as by this alone, we must be judged.”
Preamble

“That every such judgment is an express violation of the law of Christ, a daring usurpation of his throne, and a gross intrusion upon the rights and liberties of his subjects.”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• The very next sentence. “Such judgment” is the one just before it: “no man has a right to judge his brother, except in so far as he manifestly violates the express letter of the law.” Whoever judges his brother’s conscience is sitting on Christ’s throne.
Luther, a year before Worms

“…whoever comes out of the water of baptism can boast that he is already a consecrated priest, bishop, and pope…”

No one can stand before God in your place.
So no one can read the Word in your place.
Martin Luther, To the Christian Nobility of the German Nation, 1520 · Luther’s Works 44
• One click. A year before Worms: “we are all consecrated priests through baptism, as St. Peter says in I Peter 2[:9].” No one can stand before God for you.
• The sentence goes on: “although of course it is not seemly that just anybody should exercise such office.”
The Catechism

“Conscience is the aboriginal Vicar of Christ.”

John Henry Newman, 1875 · quoted in the Catechism of the Catholic Church §1778
• Let it sit. “Aboriginal” means first: before pope or council, Christ’s first representative in a person is conscience. And it is in the Catechism.
• Newman, Letter to the Duke of Norfolk (1875) §5. Same letter: “I shall drink—to the Pope, if you please,—still, to Conscience first, and to the Pope afterwards.”
Last week

Conscience is an exercise of
the priesthood of all believers.

Last week’s fifth idea, the starting point tonight. In conscience each believer stands before God with no one in between, which is what a priest does. Luther, 1520: “we are all consecrated priests through baptism.” The Catechism, §1546: “The whole community of believers is, as such, priestly.”
So conscience answers to Christ

“…every man must be allowed to judge for himself, as every man must bear his own judgment—must give account of himself to God.”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• The Address, right after “no man can judge for his brother,” echoing Romans 14:12: “every one of us shall give account of himself to God.” Romans 14:4 is the same chapter: “Who art thou that judgest another man’s servant? to his own master he standeth or falleth.”
• → If conscience is where I answer to Christ, then conscience is about Christ.
Not to the pope.
Not to a council.
Not to me.
To Christ.
Four clicks. Whom does your conscience answer to?

Christ makes us different.

Each of us answers to him, and each of us hears him imperfectly.
The careful version: our differences come from each of us answering to Christ for ourselves, through finite understanding. Not every difference is Christ’s doing; some are our errors. But the variety is what you get when Christ, not a council, is the one we answer to.

How can Christians have unity,

if Christ, working through us,
makes us so different?

One click. The question we stopped on last week, now in its sharpest form. If the source of our differences is Christ himself, no instrument can remove them: not a creed, not a council, not a sword. Pause.

We will not be united by another list.

Not of propositions, not of doctrines, not of opinions.
Christ alone means: not Christ plus a better confession. Campbell will not offer one, not even his own.

We will understand differently.

Not a failure to be fixed: it follows from each of us answering to Christ.
Campbell expected it

“…nor, indeed, is there anything either in Scripture or the nature of things that should induce us to expect an entire unity of sentiment in the present imperfect state.”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• From the Address. He does not expect us to agree on everything in this life.
And would not want it

“Nor can we conceive what desirable purpose such a unity of sentiment would serve, except to render useless some of those gracious, self-denying, and compassionate precepts of mutual sympathy and forbearance which the word of God enjoins upon his people.”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• The next sentence. He does not think it would be good if we did agree on everything: a church with no differences would have no use for forbearance. Difference is where love has work to do.

There can only be one answer.

Christ alone

One click. Say the line, let it sit, then click. Then the Preamble says it in his words.
Preamble, continued

“…nor, indeed, can we reasonably expect to find it anywhere but in Christ and his simple word, which is the same yesterday, to-day, and forever.”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• The clause you stopped before. Now it has fifteen hundred years behind it.
• → Thomas Campbell saw only one answer: given a people called to follow their conscience, given that no council could forever bind it, the only thing Christians could unite on was Christ himself.

Every time we hand a creed, a council, or a magistrate
a job only Christ can do, it fails.

The chapter’s thesis, right after Campbell’s answer (“anywhere but in Christ”). Point back at the egg: every one of those was a good instrument given the wrong job. Campbell names the job in the Address: creeds were “designed and embraced for the purpose of promoting and securing that desirable unity and purity which the Bible alone, without those helps, would be insufficient to maintain and secure.” That is the job description, and no document can do it.
→ Which is not to say confessions are bad.

There is nothing wrong with a confession.

But a confession cannot make us one.
Only Christ can do that.
Two clicks. Campbell is not against confessions. For teaching, the fuller the better (Proposition 7, next). The fault on the egg was never the confession; it was the job the confession was given: to be the boundary of the body of Christ.
Proposition 7

“…doctrinal exhibitions of the great system of Divine truths… be highly expedient, and the more full and explicit they be for those purposes, the better; yet… they ought not to be made terms of Christian communion…”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• Campbell says it himself: write the fullest confession you can. Just do not make it the door. Elided: “and defensive testimonies in opposition to prevailing errors”; “as these must be in a great measure the effect of human reasoning, and of course must contain many inferential truths.”
• The sentence ends: “the Church from the beginning did, and ever will, consist of little children and young men, as well as fathers.”

Christ already unites us.

Christ alone is the basis of unity because in Christ the church is already one. In the church, the unity is already there. We do not build it; we see it, or we fail to.
Proposition 1

“That the Church of Christ upon earth is essentially, intentionally, and constitutionally one; consisting of all those in every place that profess their faith in Christ and obedience to him in all things according to the Scriptures, and that manifest the same by their tempers and conduct, and of none else…”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• The class has heard the opening clause twice; now the whole sentence. Ask: do you believe unity is given rather than built? If so, the sects are the innovation.
Proposition 1, misread
Not only the ones with our name on the sign.
Not only Rome.
Not only Constantinople.
“All those in every place.”
Four clicks. In Church of Christ circles the first proposition is sometimes quoted to mean the opposite of what it says: only the congregations with “Church of Christ” on the sign are the true church. Some Catholic and some Orthodox thinkers say the same of their own communions. Campbell says the opposite: the church on earth consists of Christians in every denomination, sect and division. Christ has made them one; we have not.
East and West, after 1054

“We are divided, we know, but how, when, and by what authority?”

David Bentley Hart, “The Myth of Schism,” 2008
• Hart, an Eastern Orthodox theologian, on the schism of 1054. In Ecumenism Today: The Universal Church in the 21st Century, ed. Francesca Aran Murphy and Christopher Asprey (Ashgate, 2008); reprinted at clarion-journal.com (2014).
• He shows how porous the wall was for centuries: shared sacraments under the Ottomans and under communist rule, Syrian parishes in America where Catholic and Orthodox belong to “one church and one altar.” The same paragraph: “Can the failure of communion between two patriarchs or bishops… create a real division of sacramentally united communions from one another?”
Are we divided?

“…are we sure that we are? For, if not, then our division is simply sin… a fiction of the will, and obedience to a lie.”

David Bentley Hart, “The Myth of Schism,” 2008
• The full sentence: “This is not a moral question—how do we dare to remain disunited?—but a purely canonical one: are we sure that we are? For, if not, then our division is simply sin, a habit of desire and thought that feeds upon nothing but its own perverse passions and immanent logic, a fiction of the will, and obedience to a lie.”
• → The principle underneath: Christ makes the church one, and pope, bishop and council have neither the authority nor the ability to divide it. Constitutionally one, as Campbell says.
Already

“For by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body, whether we be Jews or Gentiles, whether we be bond or free; and have been all made to drink into one Spirit.”

1 Corinthians 12:13
• Paul: “are we all baptized,” past tense; the one body is a fact before it is a task.
Holding fast

“…leaning upon their Beloved, and embracing each other in him, holding fast the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace.”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• The Address. “Holding fast” the unity, not making it. Ephesians 4:3 says the same: “keep the unity of the Spirit.” You can only keep what you already have.

Do we recognize it?

Ask it and let it hang. The church is already one; do we see it? Claim three answers: recognizing it is our visible unity.
At the table

“For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord’s body.”

1 Corinthians 11:29
• Paul’s charge against the Corinthians: at the Supper they did not recognize the body of Christ in their brothers (11:17–34, the rich eating while the poor go hungry). That failure turns communion into judgment.

When Campbell gave the Supper to other Presbyterians,
he was discerning the body.

The charge of 1807: he gave communion to Presbyterians outside the Seceders. He was recognizing the body of Christ across the lines his own synod drew.

No sect ever had the authority,
or the ability, to divide what Christ has joined.

Whatever our sects and sub-sects have done with their divisions and anathemas, they never had the authority or the ability to divide the body Christ made one.
Proposition 9

“That all that are enabled through grace to make such a profession… should consider each other as the precious saints of God, should love each other as brethren, children of the same family and Father, temples of the same Spirit, members of the same body… Whom God hath thus joined together no man should dare to put asunder.”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• The marriage line: recognition is not optional. Ask: who are we not treating as brethren, and on what term?
Receive one another

“Wherefore receive ye one another, as Christ also received us to the glory of God.”

Romans 15:7
• Romans 14–15 is the passage on receiving those who differ over days and food: “Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations” (14:1).

I receive you
because Christ received you.

What we recognize in a brother is Christ’s work. So the visible unity rests on the same ground as the real one. Put anything else there, and we are receiving on some ground other than Christ.

Our first duty:
recognize what Christ has already done.

And stop pretending that anything else has taken precedence over Christ’s own declaration and work.

Christ and his word,
not our interpretations of his word.

Claim five. Last week’s sixth idea, now as the ground of unity.
Worms, 18 April 1521

“Unless I am convinced by the testimony of the Scriptures or by clear reason… I am bound by the Scriptures… and my conscience is captive to the Word of God. I cannot and will not recant anything, since it is neither safe nor right to go against conscience. May God help me. Amen.”

Martin Luther at Worms, 18 April 1521
• The whole sentence, two trims on screen: “I have quoted,” and the parenthesis “(for I do not trust either in the pope or in councils alone, since it is well known that they have often erred and contradicted themselves).” Councils have erred: the egg, in his words.
• Note how it starts: “Unless I am convinced.” He holds his own reading open to correction. That is the opposite of “I can do what I want.” (Translations vary; this is the common English form.)

Captive to the Word of God.

Not to the pope’s reading of it.
Not to a council’s.
Not even to his own.
Not to what he thinks it says.
To the Word of God itself.
Five clicks; slow down on “not even to his own.” The proof is the first clause of the sentence: “Unless I am convinced by the testimony of the Scriptures or by clear reason.” He can still be corrected by the Word, so he is not treating his own reading as the Word. What binds him is the Word itself, and his conscience is where he answers to God for how faithfully he reads it. That is why no council can do it for him: an obligation cannot be handed to someone else.

Word of God≠interpretations of the Word of God

Two clicks. What Luther is captive to. Not the pope’s reading, not a council’s, not even his own: “Unless I am convinced by the testimony of the Scriptures or by clear reason.” He can be corrected by the Word, so his reading is not the Word. That is what keeps conscience from becoming “I can do what I want”: it answers to something outside itself.

Campbell is not trading the Westminster Confession
for an agreed reading of the Bible.

How the supremacy of the Word has often been applied among us: a new legalism, as if Campbell threw out the Confession so we could all agree on one interpretation of the Bible instead. That is not what he says, and not what he can be saying.

If we cannot agree on the Westminster Confession,
how much less on all of Scripture?

Campbell knows this. United on Christ and his word means our commitment to Christ and to his word, not to a particular interpretation of it.
The Address

“With you all we desire to unite in the bonds of an entire Christian unity—Christ alone being the head, the center, his word the rule…”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• The Address. When Campbell says “Christ and his word,” listen for what he does not say.
Not Christ and our understanding of Christ.
Not Scripture and our interpretation of Scripture.
Christ, and Scripture itself.
Three clicks. Last week’s sixth idea, now as the ground of unity. We can gather around Christ and Scripture without making our readings of Scripture the test of fellowship.
The objection: no one reads Scripture without interpreting it. True, and Campbell knows it. His line is not between reading and not reading; it is between what I hold and what I require of you. Next, in his words.
Hold it. Do not require it.

“We would then no longer exalt our own opinions and inferences to an equality with express revelation, by condemning and rejecting our brother for differing with us in those things.”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• From the Address. The fault is not having opinions and inferences; it is raising them to the level of Scripture and then rejecting a brother over them.
• Proposition 3: nothing “required of them as terms of communion, but what is expressly taught and enjoined upon them in the word of God.”
• Proposition 6, from claim one: deductions “do properly belong to the after and progressive edification of the Church.”
• → Then say it plainly.

Keep your reading.
Do not make it your brother’s test.

The whole of claim five in a sentence. Then the clearest example: a creed.
How Christ leads us into truth
The Spirit. “…the Holy Spirit for our teacher and guide, to lead us into all truth…”
Scripture. “…to form their judgment by the Divine word itself, and not by any human explication of it…”
Reason. “We pretend not, therefore, to divest ourselves of reason…”
All three speak to the conscience.
Four clicks, all from the Declaration and Address: the Preamble (echoing John 16:13, “he will guide you into all truth”); the Address’s appeal to those who form their judgment by the word “humbly relying upon and looking for the promised assistance of Divine teaching”; and the Address on reason, which goes on: “nor yet, of any of its proper and legitimate operations upon Divinely revealed truths.”
→ So unanimity is reached the way Christ allows: brothers reasoning together, the Spirit working on hearts, Scripture read and shared and argued over. Never by decree.

We are united not by a shared interpretation,
but by a shared commitment to Scripture itself.

Every week I meet with Christians who understand Scripture differently than I do. We wrestle with it; sometimes we move closer, sometimes farther apart. What unites us is a shared commitment to Scripture, which is part of our shared commitment to Christ: not our interpretation of Scripture, not our interpretation of Christ, but Christ himself.

Recognize the unity Christ has already made,
and strive to act accordingly.

Where Campbell lands, and where we start.
Black.

What is beautiful here? What do we carry forward?

Backup prompts (off the slide): Who have we treated the way Luther treated Zwingli, over a reading of Scripture? What instrument do we reach for when we want unity: a statement, a rule, a vote?
If the room is slow: “Have you ever been the brother someone else judged for?”
Idea 1 of 5

Freedom of conscience is how Christ builds his body.

We cannot compel conscience, and Christ does not ask us to: each believer answers to him as a priest. Campbell: judging for a brother is “a daring usurpation of his throne.”
Idea 2 of 5

Only Christ can unite us.

If Christ is the reason for our diversity, Christ is the only one who can unite us: “anywhere but in Christ and his simple word.” Confessions teach; they cannot be the boundary of the body.
Idea 3 of 5

Christ has already made us one.

Proposition 1: “essentially, intentionally, and constitutionally one; consisting of all those in every place.” Not only us.
Idea 4 of 5

Our first duty is to recognize it.

“Not discerning the Lord’s body” (1 Corinthians 11:29). Campbell at the table with other Presbyterians: recognizing what Christ has joined.
Idea 5 of 5

Christ and his word, not our interpretations of his word.

Luther was captive to the Word of God, not to his reading of it. “Christ alone being the head, the center, his word the rule.” Keep your reading; do not make it your brother’s test.
Ideas
1.Freedom of conscience is how Christ builds his body.
2.Only Christ can unite us.
3.Christ has already made us one.
4.Our first duty is to recognize it.
5.Christ and his word, not our interpretations of his word.
All five at once, before the discussion.

Five years before this was printed, the men of Cane Ridge had already tried to live it.
Close. They built something, watched it succeed, and then did something almost without precedent in church history: they wrote a will for it. Chapter 4, October 25.

Addendum

Reference material; not part of the telling.
What every one of them had in common

Every one had a sword behind it.

Constantine · Theodosius · Marcian · Zeno · the papal legates
Charles V · the council of Zurich · Philip of Hesse · Parliament · William and Mary
the patrons · the burgess oath · the magistrate
Three clicks, back across the egg: who stood behind each instrument. Emperors convened Nicaea (Constantine), Constantinople (Theodosius I), Ephesus (Theodosius II) and Chalcedon (Marcian), and issued the Henotikon (Zeno); legates carried Rome’s bull in 1054; Charles V issued the Edict of Worms; Zurich’s council ruled and drowned; Philip of Hesse called Marburg; Parliament imposed Westminster; the crown settled 1690; Parliament’s Patronage Act made the Secession; a civic oath made the Burgher split; and the last split was over whether the magistrate may enforce religion at all.
→ Back to the egg for a moment: every instrument on it could be enforced. Luther lived under the same swords: Charles V at Worms, Philip of Hesse calling Marburg. Campbell did not, which is why he could take Worms further.
The Address · why 1809, why here

“What dreary effects of those accursed divisions are to be seen, even in this highly favored country, where the sword of the civil magistrate has not as yet learned to serve at the altar.”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• From the Evils of Division paragraph, just before “congregations broken to pieces.” The Address says it outright later: “A country happily exempted from the baneful influence of a civil establishment of any peculiar form of Christianity.”
• The First Amendment was eighteen years old; Pennsylvania had never had an established church. For the first time in the story, nobody could enforce a creed. So unity could not be imposed here. It would have to be found.
• A few decades after one Declaration of Independence, another.
Resolution IV

“That this Society by no means considers itself a Church, nor does at all assume to itself the powers peculiar to such a society… but merely as voluntary advocates for Church reformation…”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• The one resolution to keep: voluntary advocates for reform, not a new church.
The reception
October 1810 · the Synod of Pittsburgh refuses Christian and ministerial communion. Nobody joins.
• Candor beat, one click. A unity plea addressed to every party and joined, in the event, by almost no one; the synod’s refusal is Week 5’s opening.
• → And the movement it started? We know what happened next.
October 1809

Alexander, twenty-one, three weeks off the ship, reads the proof-sheets as they come from the printer.

Two sentences of Glasgow: the family wrecked off Islay, ten months in Glasgow, and the son refusing the Seceder communion token on his own, an ocean away from his father’s break. On the road from Philadelphia they find out they have each broken with the same fence, through the same table. Then the proof-sheets.
The warning

“Sir… these words, however plausible in appearance, are not sound. For if you follow these out, you must become a Baptist.”

Rev. Riddle, a neighboring Presbyterian minister, to Alexander · Richardson, Memoirs 1:251
• Alexander presses the question on his father: will these principles not mean giving up infant baptism? He buys every pro-infant-baptism treatise in Andrew Munro’s own bookshop to find out.
The answer

“We make our appeal to the law and to the testimony. Whatever is not found therein we must of course abandon.”

Thomas Campbell to his son, every time · Richardson 1:252
• The father’s answer committed the next generation before anyone knew where it led. Within three years the logic runs its course; that is a later week.
Last week · The Declaration and Address, 1809
Five clicks, about three minutes: last week in five pictures. The egg (325 to 1806, every instrument offered for unity left another division); Worms (Anton von Werner, 1877); Marburg (August Noack, 1867–69); the drowning (Jan Luyken, Martyrs Mirror, 1685); Thomas Campbell.
Last week’s ideas
1.Unity is the design of religion.
2.Division is a horrid evil.
3.Every instrument failed.
4.Conscience cannot be compelled.
5.Conscience is an exercise of the priesthood of all believers.
6.Commitment to the Word of God, not interpretations of the Word of God.
7.No one may judge for his brother.
Last week’s seven ideas, all at once. Read them, or let the room read them; do not re-teach.
The record

“And here we would ask: Have all or any of those human compilations been able to prevent divisions, to heal breaches, or to produce and maintain unity of sentiment even among those who have most firmly and solemnly embraced them?”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• From the Address. The egg in one sentence: every confession on it was signed, and every one split.
Not even his own

“Let none imagine that the subjoined propositions are at all intended as an overture toward a new creed or standard for the Church, or as in any wise designed to be made a term of communion; nothing can be further from our intention.”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• Just before the thirteen propositions. He refuses to let his own list become the next one.
One mind would need one understanding

“…it appears highly questionable whether such a thing can at all be secured, by any expedient whatsoever, especially if we consider that it necessarily presupposes in so far a unity or sameness of understanding.”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• From the Address, on “unity of sentiment.” Agreement on every point would require us all to understand alike, and no expedient can produce that.

So difference of understanding
cannot be a boundary of unity.

If we will inevitably understand differently, then a boundary drawn at understanding will divide the church forever. Campbell draws it in two propositions.
We cannot compel anyone
farther than they understand.
We cannot compel anyone
farther than they are required to understand.
Two clicks. The first is Proposition 6: an inference binds a conscience only as far as it sees the connection. The second is Proposition 8: no one need understand everything to belong, so no one may be required to profess more than they know.
Proposition 6

“That although inferences and deductions from Scripture premises, when fairly inferred, may be truly called the doctrine of God’s holy word, yet are they not formally binding upon the consciences of Christians farther than they perceive the connection… Therefore, no such deductions can be made terms of communion…”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• Conscience again, now as polity. You cannot believe what you do not see, so you cannot be made to. Every council on the egg was an inference made a term of communion.
Proposition 8

“That as it is not necessary that persons should have a particular knowledge or distinct apprehension of all Divinely revealed truths in order to entitle them to a place in the Church; neither should they, for this purpose, be required to make a profession more extensive than their knowledge…”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• The one that answers Chalcedon directly: no term that excludes those who cannot understand it. The rest of the sentence: “a profession of their faith in and obedience to him, in all things, according to his word, is all that is absolutely necessary to qualify them for admission into his Church.”

Christ is the basis of our visible unity.

The unity is real before we see it; it becomes visible when we receive each other: at the table, in the pulpit, in the name “brother.”
What the world sees

“This gracious unity and unanimity in Jesus would afford the best external evidence of their union with him, and of their conjoint interest in the Father’s love.”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• From the Address. Visible unity is the evidence of an invisible union. What the world is meant to see is Christ.
The prayer

“That they all may be one… that the world may believe that thou hast sent me.”

John 17:21
• The prayer the Address echoes: a prayer, not a command, and for the sake of the world’s belief.

Christ is the basis of unanimity.

Claim four. We are different now; Christ leads us toward one mind over time. The question is how.
Unanimity matters

“In so far, then, as this holy unity and unanimity in faith and love is attained, just in the same degree is the glory of God and the happiness of men promoted and secured.”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• Do not let anyone hear tonight as “doctrine does not matter.” Campbell wants agreement: unanimity is good, and the more the better. The question is only how it is reached.
Not by decree

“It is not the voice of the multitude, but the voice of truth, that has power with the conscience; that can produce rational conviction and acceptable obedience.”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• From the Address, on a General Council. Fiat cannot compel the conscience, and must not try. A vote, a council, a decree: none of them reaches the place where belief happens. “Rational conviction” and “acceptable obedience”: only truth produces those.

And yes, this is difficult.

That is how community works.
It is especially how Christian community works.
Two clicks. Say it plainly: it would be easier to sign a paper. Living with brothers who read the same Bible and see differently takes patience, and Campbell says so.
Forbearance

“Ought they not, therefore, to bear with each other—‘to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace; forbearing one with another in love?’”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• From the Address, quoting Ephesians 4:2–3. The word he keeps returning to. Forbearance is not indifference: you only bear with what you actually disagree with.

Different is not divided.

The conclusion of the argument. Forbearance is how different stays undivided. Division is something else: it is what we do when we will not bear the difference. Last week: “a horrid evil.”
Today

We have more visible unity than they did in 1809.

Is it because we have extended love?
Or because we have stopped caring?
Or have we just started dividing over different things?
Three clicks; take answers after each.
• More unity: in 1807 Thomas Campbell himself was charged by his presbytery for giving the Supper to Presbyterians outside the Seceders; suspended in February 1808, then rebuked and admonished by the synod that May. Since then: the World Council of Churches (1948); Vatican II’s decree on ecumenism (1964), which accepts baptized Protestants as brothers; Lutheran–Catholic Joint Declaration on Justification (1999); full communion among Lutherans, Presbyterians, Reformed and UCC (1997). Most churches now welcome any baptized believer to the table.
• Stopped caring: denominational loyalty has collapsed; people switch churches over music or childcare. Christian Smith’s “moralistic therapeutic deism” (Soul Searching, 2005): if nothing much is believed, there is nothing to divide over.
• New lines: the old lines were doctrine and polity; the new ones run through sexuality and politics. The United Methodist Church lost about a quarter of its U.S. congregations, 2019–2023; the Anglican Church in North America formed in 2009. Many congregations now sort by party more than by creed.
→ Campbell would not accept the second answer: forbearance only means something if you care.
Campbell wanted both

“…manifesting to each other their mutual charity and zeal for the truth.”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• From the Address. Charity without zeal is indifference; zeal without charity is the egg. Campbell asks for both at once.
Charged with indifference

“…we intend to go just as far as it will suffer us, but not one hair-breadth further…”

Declaration and Address, 1809
• The charge in his day was “Latitudinarianism”: that unity this broad means nothing matters. His answer, in the Address: “If this be Latitudinarianism, it must be a good thing… for we are told, ‘the commandment is exceeding broad;’ and we intend to go just as far as it will suffer us, but not one hair-breadth further.” That is not indifference; it is a fence drawn exactly where Scripture draws it.
The Churches of Christ

We have kept dividing.

We have all lived it.
Does that mean Thomas Campbell was wrong?
Two clicks. Let the first one sit: everyone in the room has a story of a split, a congregation, a family. Look back at the tree: one cup, non-class, non-institutional, instrumental, premillennial. Then ask the question and let them answer before the next slide.

No. It means he was right.

Every division since has come from someone
offering another answer than Christ.
There is no other answer. There never will be.
Two clicks. Campbell diagnosed the problem correctly; the divisions are what it looks like when his point is not taken as deeply as it merits. Cups, classes, institutions, instruments, the millennium: every one was made a term of communion, asked to do the job only Christ can do. It did what every instrument on the egg did.
Our table

What do we require of someone before they sit at our table?

Discussion, eight minutes. Have them list what we actually require. Then proposition 8 against the list: which of these is a profession more extensive than their knowledge? Every room has its Munro item; ours is not infant baptism. Leave it open. Set it against the Evils list: division already costs that; what would unity cost?
The measure

“…neither should they… be required to make a profession more extensive than their knowledge…”

Proposition 8
• Hold their list against this. Which of these is a profession more extensive than their knowledge?
